fuk_001: You can recognise it by its dense, pyramid-shaped green crown, 21.5 metres tall with a trunk 4.9 metres round. It stands beside the main hall of Kashii Shrine.
fuk_002: You can recognise it by its hollow lower trunk and cut-back limbs, propped and ringed with metal, turning a dense cone of gold each November. It stands beside the Gion Yamakasa starting point at Kushida Shrine.
fuk_003: You can recognise it by its base splitting into three separate stems, and by blooming earliest of the shrine's six thousand plums, from late January. It stands at Dazaifu Tenmangu.
fuk_006: You can recognise it by its deeply fluted, hollow-based trunk, 11.7 metres round and 28.5 metres tall, the largest camphor here. It stands west of the Seishinkan at Dazaifu Tenmangu.
fuk_007: You can recognise it by its full, dense, unbroken crown, about 15 metres round and 30 metres tall, a single trunk despite its name. It stands at Umi Hachimangu, about 100 metres from its companion camphor.
fuk_008: You can recognise it by its huge girth, about 20 metres round, its upper trunk gone and a large rough cavity open in the side. It stands at Umi Hachimangu, about 100 metres from its companion camphor.
fuk_009: You can recognise it by its heavy, scarred trunk, hollow inside, with the crown stopping abruptly where lightning snapped it off in 1914. It stands west of the main buildings at Dazaifu Tenmangu.
fuk_010: You can recognise them by the three large ginkgos standing together opposite the main hall, a few steps from the shrine's more famous single ginkgo. They stand at Kushida Shrine.
fuk_012: You can recognise it by its thick trunk, 4.4 metres round and 14 metres tall, with a root spread 8 metres across and a hollow sometimes used by a nesting owl. It stands in Kanatake, Nishi Ward.
fuk_013: You can recognise the camphor by its trunk forking into two from a single base near the ground, cords tied to its shimenawa rope. It flanks one side of the torii at Torikai Hachimangu, the ginkgo 12 metres away.
fuk_014: You can recognise it by the stone monument to the novel Ten to Sen standing beside it, marking where it was craned in whole, roots and all, in 2008. It stands in front of Nishitetsu-Kashii Station.
fuk_015: You can recognise it by its ring of more than twenty root suckers rising from one base, no single trunk to put a tape around. It stands beside a mountain-god shrine at Shimo-ose, Fuji-cho, Saga City.
